title: A tiny Pacific country rolls out universal basic income

vocab.articleQuote: The Marshall Islands uses an American windfall to pay every citizen
vocab.meaning: A windfall is a large amount of money you did not expect or work for. The word comes from fruit blown off a tree by the wind: it just lands in your lap. In the article, the money America pays the Marshall Islands is the windfall.
examples: Grandma's surprise birthday check was a windfall, and I spent it on a new bike.
The team got a windfall when a local store gave them free uniforms.

vocab.articleQuote: unconditional government payment given to all citizens as a supplement to or replacement for wages
vocab.meaning: A supplement is something added to what you already have, to make it more complete. It adds to the main thing and does not replace it. In the article, the payment would be extra money on top of a person's wages.
examples: My allowance is a supplement to the money I earn walking the neighbor's dog.
The teacher gave us a supplement to the textbook with extra practice problems.

vocab.articleQuote: The Marshallese government argues that deciding who should qualify would be costly and cumbersome.
vocab.meaning: Something cumbersome is slow, clumsy, and awkward to deal with because it is big or has too many steps. In the article, checking every person to decide who qualifies would take so much work that the government says it is not worth it.
examples: Carrying a huge cardboard box up three flights of stairs was cumbersome.
The game's rules were so cumbersome that we gave up before the first turn.

concepts.name: GDP
concepts.articleQuote: The cost of it amounts to a whopping 8% or so of GDP, but is paid from an American trust fund
concepts.meaning:
How do you say whether a country's money plan is big or small? A bag of $800 sounds small. But for a tiny country, it can be huge. To compare fairly, economists measure the size of a whole economy with **GDP**, short for *gross domestic product*. It is the total value of everything made and sold inside a country in one year: every haircut, burger, phone and bus ride.

Say your school holds a bake sale and every class sells cookies, cupcakes and lemonade. Add up all the money from all the stands, and you have the sale's "GDP".

Now imagine the principal says, "We will spend $50 on prizes." If the whole sale made $100, that is half of everything. If it made $10,000, that is tiny. Saying a cost is a **percent of GDP** tells you how heavy it is for that country.

So the takeaway: when you hear a big number, ask what share of the country's GDP it is.

concepts.name: Inflation
concepts.articleQuote: Inflation, another common concern with cash transfers, has risen
concepts.meaning:
Why might handing out money make everything cost more? That is the worry about **inflation**, a word from economics for prices across a whole economy rising over time. The word comes from *inflate*, to blow up like a balloon: the same dollar buys less.

Imagine your class has 10 slices of pizza at a party and each kid has $1, so a slice costs $1. Now the teacher secretly gives every kid another $1, but there are still only 10 slices. Everyone wants to pay more to get one, so the price drifts up to $2. Nothing about the pizza changed. There was just more money chasing the same amount of stuff.

Prices can also rise for other reasons, like a war that makes oil or food harder to get. In the article, officials say that is mostly what happened here.

So the takeaway: when prices go up, ask whether people got more money, or whether there is less stuff to buy.

quiz.question: What makes the Marshall Islands' basic income the first of its kind, according to the article?
options: It is paid by a whole country to all citizens, including children
It is paid only to people who lose their jobs
It is paid only to people living on the capital island
It is paid in goods rather than money
quiz.explanation: The article says it is believed to be the world's first national scheme paying every citizen, children included.

quiz.question: Where does the money for the payments come from?
options: A tax on tourists
An American trust fund tied to an agreement with the United States
A loan from the IMF
Fees paid by fishing boats
quiz.explanation: The cost is paid from an American trust fund, part of the compact with America.

quiz.question: Why does the article say the payment is not meant to replace work?
options: Everyone on the islands already has a job
Workers are not allowed to receive it
It is only about a tenth of income per person, so it is not nearly big enough
It is paid only once
quiz.explanation: At around $800 a year, it is only about a tenth of the country's income per person.

quiz.question: Why does the Marshallese government say it pays everyone instead of only those in need?
options: Deciding who qualifies would be costly and cumbersome
The law forbids choosing people
Rich people asked for it
The payments are too small to matter
quiz.explanation: The government argues that working out who should qualify would be costly and cumbersome.

quiz.question: If a cost is "8% of GDP," what does that tell you?
options: It will happen in 8 years
It equals 8 percent of everything the country makes in a year
Prices rose by 8 percent
8 percent of people receive it
quiz.explanation: GDP measures the value of everything a country produces in a year, so a percent of GDP shows the size of a cost.
